newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Life is no "Bitch" for Meredith Brooks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Life is no "Bitch" for Meredith Brooks.

text.p: For a self-confessed "bitch," Meredith Brooks is smiling a lot these days.

The singer/guitarist/songwriter is sitting near the top of the charts with her new album, "Blurring the Edges," and its first single, "Bitch." The colourful video recently received two MTV Video Music Award nominations and Brooks plans to tour the country in August following a worldwide press tour.

Success has been a long time coming for the Corvallis, Oregon, native who moved to Los Angeles about eight years ago and released several independent albums. In the late 1980s, she joined a trio called the Graces, a female version of Crosby Stills & Nash, but it disbanded after one album.
She signed to Capitol Records in November 1995, by which stage she had already written most of the songs that would turn up on the album.

"Bitch," No. 2 on the U.S. singles charts for three weeks in a row, is a song about the lack of self-acceptance, with a chorus that goes: "I'm a bitch, I'm a lover, I'm a child, I'm a mother, I'm a sinner, I'm a saint, I do not feel ashamed." As such, it serves as an appropriate outlet for the New Age philosophies and Jungian ideals Brooks loves to espouse.

"We all end to wear these masks -- Hi! I'm doing fine, and Hi! I'm really cool," she said in a recent interview with Reuters at her neighbourhood coffeehouse in Los Angeles. "But the point is if you take off the mask at any moment in a day you feel sad, angry, a bitch, whatever. So I decided to change the meaning of the word and people get it."
A FEW DIDN'T GET IT

A few retailers did not "get it," in fact, and asked Capitol to supply copies of the single with "Bitch-free" artwork. "What do I care?" Brooks asked. "The song's still the song. I don't care if it says 'Bitch' on the cover or not."

The word still has a lot of stigma attached to it and opponents of "gangsta rap" complain about its omnipresence in that genre, but Brooks says people call each other bitches "all over the place in a very endearing way."

She also believes she is doing her bit for relationships. "I think this was a very freeing experience for all men because they feel like now somebody is admitting it:'I knew you had, like, a thousand moods, and Meredith said so.' I'm going like, 'Yeah, and so do you, and we just need to be more accepting and less judgmental.'"
The album's title means to live in a parallel universe, which may explain to less enlightened folks why Brooks sounds sometimes as if she were living on another planet.
But she makes no apologies. She has bounced back from severe depression and says if she were not a musician she would be doing full-time psychology seminars helping to fix people's "broken parts."

The song's -- indeed the album's -- confessional tone means that some critics are judging her in the same light as Alanis Morissette, the 23-year-old wunderkind who bared her soul on the multi-million-selling album, "Jagged Little Pill." This is an occupational hazard for a slew of white female musicians such as Jewel, Tracy Bonham, Fiona Apple and Paula Cole but Brooks brushes off the comparison and cites artists such as Chrissie Hynde, U2 and Tom Petty as huge influences.
THIRTYSOMETHING

Although some sources give Brooks' age as 31, a one-time musical colleague told Reuters she is past her mid-30's and has always been paranoid about revealing her age. Brooks clammed up on this subject in the interview but pointed out helpfully that she is "a complete and total Gemini."

It helped that Shelly Peiken, a songwriting friend with whom Brooks co-wrote six of the album's 12 songs including "Bitch," was a Gemini too. She helped transport Brooks back to painful experiences and distil them into verses and choruses.

"Bitch" was actually recorded with producer Geza X before the Capitol deal but the label fired the Los Angeles punk veteran because it felt he was taking too long on the rest of the album. David Ricketts, whose credits include Toni Childs and Sheryl Crow, took over producing duties.
"He basically cocooned me at his house for ... about 4-5 months and didn't let me see much of the world during that time. He kept people away, that's how we did it," Brooks said.

The resulting product, on which Brooks played all the lead guitar, boasts a celebratory feel, as if it has allowed her to let go of the past. It stands at No. 26 on the charts, having sold about 500,000 copies, and is likely to get a boost from the tour and successive singles.

Brooks plans to work it for the next 18 months, with all the gusto she can summon. "When you're in your creative place, when you're in the zone, it just feels great," she gushed. "You don't think about it, you're just there."
